newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani stocks seen sinking in sea of troubles.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani stocks seen sinking in sea of troubles.

text.p: Pakistani stocks, hit by a stream of bad political and economic news, are likely to slide further in the next few weeks, brokers said on Wednesday.

"We believe that the perception of the situation will shift from bad to worse, and recommend investors to stay away from the market until the situation clears in a month or so," analyst Kalim Aziz of ING Baring Securities said.
The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index tumbled 1.51 percent on Wednesday, slipping below the 1,400-point barrier to end at 1,381.96 points ahead of a one-day opposition strike.
Opposition parties have called for a nationwide strike on Thursday to protest at last Friday's killing of Murtaza Bhutto, estranged brother of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.
Murtaza, 42, was killed in a shootout between Karachi police and his supporters, seven of whom also died. His followers say police ambushed him. Police say his guards fired first.
On Monday, gunmen attacked a Sunni Moslem mosque in Multan, in Punjab province, killing 21 people and wounding many more.
The market received another shock on Tuesday when it learned that the U.S.-based Moody's Investors Service Inc had placed Pakistan credit ratings under review for a possible downgrade.

Dealer Hassan Dawar of Global Securities said the spate of bad news was likely to drive the market to a new trough. "The market seems to be heading towards a new year-low and if it falls below that, who knows where it will stop?" he said.
The index, which touched 1,332.14 points on September 10, hit a record low of 1,323.53 points last November.
Bhutto's government, in power since October 1993, is also beset by political and economic troubles.
President Farooq Leghari asked the government and opposition on Monday to form a parliamentary committee to investigate corruption charges against politicians and civil servants.

On Saturday, Leghari, a long-time Bhutto ally, asked the Supreme Court for its opinion on whether he was obliged to accept the prime minister's advice on judicial appointments, publicly airing his differences with Bhutto for the first time.
Newspapers said he had agreed to meet opposition leader Nawaz Sharif in Islamabad on Thursday.
"These separate initiatives by the president appear to be aimed at distancing himself from the Bhutto government," Aziz said. "We are seeing the ruling party at its weakest hour."
Dealers said the stock market could shake off its blues only if the political scene stabilised and talks with the International Monetary Fund in Washington proved positive.
A delegation led by V.A. Jafarey, Bhutto's adviser on finance, was due to meet IMF officials this week to try to persuade them to resume payments of a $600 million standby loan.
The IMF has held up disbursements because of doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed policies and confusion surrounding the budget for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June).
